answer.summary: Weaver recommends choosing intentionally rather than optimizing for an easy tomorrow: ask what your future self would want you to do, expect a difficult period, and act despite normal fear and uncertainty. [S1, S2, S3, S4]

sections.heading: Get out of autopilot and choose a direction
sections.content: Create space to ask where you want your life to go, what matters to you, and what your values are; consider what you will wish you had started 10 years from now, then work backward from that. Weaver also suggests asking, in your career, what you would do if you knew you would not fail (within reason). [S4, S5]

sections.heading: Use your future self to guide the hard decision
sections.content: Ask what the version of yourself five years from now would wish you would do right now. Weaver’s example is leaving a toxic relationship even though the next two months may be painful. The point is not to choose based only on what makes tomorrow easier. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Expect difficulty, and do not wait to feel ready
sections.content: He says meaningful change often gets worse before it gets better: even starting to work out may feel unpleasant at first, and people can plateau when they will not face a hard day, month, week, or year. Fear, feeling unready, and not knowing the full path are normal; waiting for a perfectly safe moment can mean never acting. [S1, S2, S3]

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately attributes to Weaver the advice to ask what your five-years-from-now self would want you to do, expect change to feel worse or uncomfortable at first, and act rather than optimize only for an easier tomorrow. Its additional points about autopilot and waiting to feel ready are also supported by the cited context.
